text.p: Australian private new capital expenditure (capex) rose a seasonally adjusted 0.9 percent in the September quarter, according to data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics.
This compares with median forecasts for a 3.0 percent fall and estimates ranging from down 15 percent to up 2.5 percent.
The data also included the fourth estimate for business investment intentions for 1996/97, which rose 7.8 percent over the third estimate to A$42.91 billion.
ANDREW PEASE, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NOMURA RESEARCH:

"One thing I think today's numbers certainly show is that the official forecasts are now looking better than they were a few weeks ago. In terms of what this means for the Reserve Bank it certainly does reduce the chances of a further easing. The one (survey) which we got today is usually the crucial survey and that is the one which usually has the highest degree of accuracy and based on today's results that certainly makes me much more confident about the investment outcome this financial year. This week we are probably going to get some important data from the Department of Industrial Relations which is the enterprise bargaining outcome for the September quarter of this year and I thin
SHANE OLIVER, CHIEF ECONOMIST, AMP SOCIETY:

"The outcome was a little bit stronger than the market expected ... it's positive that the surprise was in plant and equipment spending. I guess the implications from all of that ... given that that's an input to September quarter GDP, it suggests that you're probably going to see a positive contribution to growth from business investment. I'd say a mild positive (contribution) which would support, along with other things, growth still being reasonable in the September quarter. It is suggesting that there will definitely be growth in business investment through 96/97. It tells us probably that capital expenditure growth will be reasonable to solid in the first half of the (calendar) year
TIM PFITZNER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, NATIONAL AUSTRALIA BANK:

"I would be interested to see if there are any revisions to the June quarter. I agree that the September quarter number is a touch on the high side and we expected that it would be down a couple of percent but I just wonder whether we are working off a lower base here. Of course we will have to see what comes out in the national accounts numbers. It would still seem from our point of view if we look at the capital imports numbers that we are still looking at softer business investment (for 1996/97)."

"The key issue is investment expectations which have remained firm and consistent with the government's budget investment forecasts. Secondly, it is going to lead people to revise upwards their preliminary GDP forecasts, and that could be up by 0.4 percent for GDP(E), as well as reduce market perceptions of the probablity of a third rate cut."
IVAN CALHOUN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, DEUTSCHE MORGAN GRENFELL:

"It came out at A$42.9 billion. What it says to us is ... at least the expectation is consistent with the government's forecast for business investment. From that point of view, I think it takes away the possibility that there could be another easing in December."
MATTHEW DRENNAN, ECONOMIST, AXIOM FUNDS MANAGEMENT:

"The Q3 outcome of 0.9 percent means it's supportive of a comfortable sort of GDP outcome of 0.5 percent, or higher. It's underpinning that growth and from the interest rate perspective it is the surprising strength in the expectations for 1996/97. It's jumped from 12.5 pct to 19 pct and that means the RBA, which will be focusing much more on the leading indicators than the lagging Q3, will be much more comfortable about the fact that the interest rate easings they've done to date have underpinned confidence for the business community with continued investment supportive of pulling the economy out of the current flat spot."
